opus-5.5.text:
Oh, a lot, actually. Speed matters more than people expect. When I'm working with a coding agent, the bottleneck often isn't whether the model can eventually get the right answer. It's whether I stay in the flow while it's working. If a response takes thirty seconds, I'm still engaged; I'm reading along and thinking about the next step. If it takes five minutes, I've switched to Slack or something else, and the context-switching cost is real.

There's also a qualitative shift, not just a quantitative one. When the model is fast enough, you use it differently. You try more things. You say, "Let's try three approaches and see which one works," because each attempt is cheap. You iterate in small steps instead of writing one giant prompt and hoping it nails everything. That changes the whole interaction pattern.

Coming from the systems side, this is something I think about a lot. Inference speed isn't just a cost-saving thing for providers. It directly changes the user experience and what's possible. With agents especially, you have these long chains of tool calls, reading files, running tests, and editing code, and latency compounds across every step. So if you can make each step two or three times faster, the end-to-end task can feel dramatically different.

That said, I wouldn't trade much quality for it. If a faster model makes subtle mistakes I have to debug later, that's a net loss. The ideal is the same intelligence, just faster, and that's where a lot of the work on kernels, attention, and serving efficiency comes in. That's the part I find really exciting: those gains go straight to how productive people feel.

r001.rationale: The response says speed matters greatly and improves productivity, but it does not state that Tri Dao would pay more for faster Claude Code responses.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot. It's probably the thing I notice most day to day. When I'm working in Claude Code, I'm in a loop: I ask for something, I look at what comes back, I correct it or push it further. If each step takes a couple of seconds, I stay in flow and the whole thing feels like a conversation. If each step takes thirty seconds, I context-switch, I open another tab, and when I come back I've lost some of the thread. The quality of the model matters enormously, but latency changes how I use it. With a fast model I'll ask small, exploratory questions that I'd never bother with if I had to wait.

And this is kind of the thing I've spent my career on from the other side. FlashAttention, Mamba, the inference work, a lot of it is ultimately about making generation cheaper and faster, because faster isn't just a convenience. It changes what's economically and practically possible. If you can decode tokens quickly and cheaply, you can afford to let the model think longer, run more tool calls, explore multiple approaches, and still get back to the user in a reasonable time. So speed and intelligence aren't really separate axes. Speed is a budget, and you can spend that budget on more reasoning.

That said, for coding specifically, I'd still take a slower model that's right over a fast one that's wrong, because the cost of debugging a confident mistake is way higher than the cost of waiting. What I actually want is the ability to choose. For quick refactors or "what does this function do," give me the fast path. For something architectural where it needs to read half the repo, I'm happy to wait. The ideal is a system that figures out which mode I'm in without me having to ask.

r001.rationale: The response says faster Claude Code responses matter a lot and describes their benefits, but it does not say Tri Dao would be willing to pay more for them.
